claims.text: LPBF-produced high-entropy-alloy components currently exhibit dimensional mismatches.
LPBF-produced high-entropy-alloy components currently exhibit significant porosity and hot cracking.
LPBF-produced high-entropy-alloy components have non-uniform microstructures that compromise mechanical performance.
A closed-loop machine-learning system can monitor melt-pool behavior and thermal gradients and dynamically modulate laser power and scan speed.
Laser power and scan speed are process variables relevant to HEA build or cladding quality.
Power and velocity data can be used alongside defect outcomes to develop defect-prediction frameworks for HEA LPBF.
HEA laser additive manufacturing operates under rapid-quench or high-cooling-rate conditions.
Cantor-type Co-Cr-Fe-Mn-Ni alloys are prominent HEA systems in LPBF research datasets.
Adaptive modulation of energy input will enhance melt-pool stability.
Adaptive modulation of energy input will improve microstructural homogenization.
Real-time parameter adjustment can compensate for rapid thermal gradients and fluctuating melt-pool dynamics.
Dynamic closed-loop control will reduce porosity and hot-cracking formation.
Dynamic closed-loop control will produce a better balance between fusion quality and geometric fidelity.
Closed-loop ML control will reduce defect density relative to static process control.
Closed-loop ML control will improve dimensional agreement with CAD models relative to static process control.
Closed-loop ML control will improve tensile strength and hardness relative to static process control.
Current static process control provides only limited concurrent improvements in dimensional precision and mechanical performance.
The benefit of adaptive control depends on adequate sensor resolution and control-system response time.
Extreme energy inputs or highly unstable melt conditions may exceed the adaptive system's ability to compensate.
